newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Poor indicators cloud Thai economic picture.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Poor indicators cloud Thai economic picture.

text.p: The latest monthly economic data released by the Bank of Thailand on Thursday painted a distinctly cloudy portrait of the economy with widened deficits in the balance of payments, current account and trade balance.
But a silver lining was evident with an improvement in the latest monthly export figures, the manufacturing production index and price stability.

Thailand's troubled economy has been riddled with problems recently. Gross domestic product growth for 1997 is officially seen at a decade-low 5.9 percent against 6.4 percent posted in 1996. Private economists see a much lower rate.

The country's finance sector is going through a terrible spell, hit by over-exposure to the depressed property sector, which has has been hammered by a glut and liquidity woes. High interest rates have stifled business and exports have turned sluggish.

The central bank said balance of payments remained in the red for the third month in a row, with the April deficit doubling to 15.5 billion baht ($596.1 million) from around 700 million baht in March.
The March trade deficit widened to 22.2 billion baht in March against 21.7 billion in February.
The March current account deficit widened to 15.9 billion baht from 14.7 billion, but analysts said this was still low by Thai standards.
Kleothong Hetrakul, the central bank's chief economist, declined to elaborate on the causes for the widening of the balance of payments deficit, saying details were not yet available.

"We don't have all the details yet on what the major cause for the rise in the deficit is -- imports, exports, imported capital or service balance. By next month we should have a clearer picture," she told a news conference.
However, judging from the first-quarter figure, a sharp drop in non-resident baht accounts held by foreigners could be a major reason for the deficit, Kleothong said.
"But the capital inflows from foreign direct investment, which accounted for 25 percent of all investment, has grown by 12 percent during the first quarter," she added.

"In the past, we were used to an influx of short-term capital inflows which were more than we needed to finance the current account deficit. This kind of capital caused us problems in the short term," she said.

But analysts said the wider balance of payment deficit showed that the country was under pressure from a reduction of short-term capital flows that had not been offset sufficiently by an improvement in long-term flows.

Kleothong said that despite the present shortfalls, the central bank was confident that Thailand would be able to finance its current account gap, as capital flows were expected to improve on an anticipated economic recovery later this year.
"We believe that, with all the necessary measures taken by the government, the economy will show signs of recovery in the third and fourth quarters," she said.
She said the March manufacturing production index, which rose 6.4 percent year-on-year versus a 3.0 percent rise in February, pointed toward a positive trend for exports.
The index was mainly pushed up by increased production of export-oriented canned seafood and the textile industry.

Thai exports rose 4.8 percent to 126.9 billion baht in March against a contraction of 5.5 percent in February, the central bank said. Thailand's export growth has been sluggish recently after a 0.2 percent contraction in 1996 against a 23.6 percent rise in 1995.
